{{nihongo|'''Anagiri Daijinja'''|穴切大神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Kai Province]].

'''Anagiri Ōjinja''' (あなぎりだいじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} located in Takara 2-chōme, {{ill|Kōfu|Q201932|qid=Q201932}}, {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|Q132720|qid=Q132720}}. It is associated with the lake-water legend and the “Kekiretsu” (mountain-splitting) legend of the {{ill|Kōfu Basin|Q11577819|qid=Q11577819}}. Its former shrine rank was {{ill|Gō-sha|ja|郷社|qid=Q134917316}}.

The shrine stands in the northern part of the Kōfu Basin, at the western edge of Kōfu’s central area, on the left bank of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Aikawa}} flowing north–south through the western part of the city.

=== Enshrined deities ===
The shrine enshrines three deities: {{ill|Ōkuninushi|lt=Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto|qid=Q276944}} (Ōkuninushi), {{ill|Sukunabikona|ca|Sukunabikona|fr|Sukunabikona|it|Sukuna-hikona|ja|スクナビコナ|ko|스쿠나비코나|mni|ꯁꯨꯀꯨꯅꯕꯤꯀꯣꯅ|pl|Sukunabikona|pt|Sukunahikona|simple|Sukunabikona|sv|Suku-Na-Bikona|zh|少彥名|qid=Q3275687|lt=Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto}}, and {{ill|Susanoo-no-Mikoto|lt=Susanoo-no-Mikoto|qid=Q272993}}.

Until the early modern period it was commonly called “Anagiri Myōjin,” and in connection with the lake-water legend there is a theory that the original deity was Anagiri Myōjin or possibly Kekiretsu Myōjin.<ref name="斎藤">Saitō, “Anagiri Ōjinja.”</ref>

=== History ===
According to the *{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kaikoku Shaki–Jiki}}* (hereafter *Shaki*), the shrine was originally called Kurotona Shrine, but later received the divine title “Anagiri Daimyōjin” from the {{ill|Imperial Court of Japan|ja|朝廷 (日本)|qid=Q30253177}}. It identifies the shrine as the *shikinaisha* “Kurotona Shrine” listed in the *{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}*, and the *{{ill|Kaikokushi|Q11577871|qid=Q11577871}}* (hereafter *Kokushi*), vol. 55, Shrine Section I, also introduces the Kurotona Shrine theory citing the *Shaki*. However, as discussed below, the location of the shrine in the era of the *Jinmyōchō* appears to have belonged to {{ill|Koma District|Q11479803|qid=Q11479803}}.<ref>The *Kokushi* itself identifies the Kurotona Shrine as a *shikinaisha* with Kurotona Shrine (Karato Myōjin) in Kurashina Village (present-day Kurashina, Makioka Town, {{ill|Yamanashi (city)|Q840610|qid=Q840610}}), and there is also a theory identifying it with Kurotona Shrine (Kurobe Myōjin) in Kurodaira Village (present-day Kurodaira Town, Kōfu City). These two shrines are regarded as leading candidates as disputed shrines (*ronsha*) (see *Shikinaisha Chōsa Hōkoku*, vol. 10, Kōgakkan University Press, 1981).</ref>

Both works present as the shrine’s origin the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kai Province Lake-Water Legend}}, also known as the Kekiretsu legend, in which the Kōfu Basin was once a great lake that was drained by cutting through mountains. According to the *Shaki*, during the {{ill|Wadō (era)|Q1373026|qid=Q1373026}} (early 8th century), the provincial governor of {{ill|Kai Province|Q858076|qid=Q858076}} proposed converting the lake into arable land, petitioned the Imperial Court, and prayed to Ōkuninushi (Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto), a god of nation-building. He then cut through the basin’s southern area at Kajikazawa-guchi ({{ill|Fujikawa, Yamanashi|Q1351723|qid=Q1351723}}), drained the water into the {{ill|Fuji River|Q596110|qid=Q596110}}, and carried out a major project to turn the basin into rice paddies. Upon completion, Ōnamuchi-no-Mikoto, who had granted divine aid, was ceremonially enshrined as the shrine’s founding deity. The provincial governor who led the development was also worshiped as Kekiretsu Myōjin in the Kawauchi region along the Fuji River. It is also said that the regional name “Kawauchi” derives from “kawaochi” (river falling).<ref>*Yamanashi Encyclopedia (Revised and Expanded Edition)*, “Anagiri Ōjinja” (Yamanashi Nichinichi Shimbun, 1989).</ref>

On the other hand, the *Kokushi* records a different tradition: that three deities drained the basin’s lake—first one kicked through the mountain ridge, the next bored a hole through the mountain to release the water, and the last guided the water to the Fuji River to form river channels. The first deity was called Kekiretsu Myōjin, the second Anagiri Myōjin, and the last Setachi Fudō. Citing an “old record,” it states that this shrine enshrines the second deity and that the name “Anagiri” derives from this act, concluding that “those who achieved flood-control works in ancient times were enshrined and revered as gods and Buddhas.”

Throughout {{ill|Yamanashi Prefecture|Q132720|qid=Q132720}}, many legends remain that the basin was once a lake and was developed through divine or Buddhist power. Geologically, the Kōfu Basin is thought to have once been an inlet of {{ill|Suruga Bay|Q1201023|qid=Q1201023}}, later shaped into its present form through {{ill|Fold (geology)|Q81659|qid=Q81659}} and volcanic activity. In the early modern period, the area including the shrine site—then part of Nishi-Aonuma Village<ref>The village area corresponds to present-day Takara 1–2 chōme, Marunouchi 2–3 chōme, Kotobuki-chō, and Aioi 1–2 chōme.</ref>—is considered a place-name remnant of Aonuma-gō in Koma District listed in the *{{ill|Wamyō Ruijushō|Q2702542|qid=Q2702542}}*. The name “Aonuma” is also said to derive from the many lakes and marshes that once dotted the area.<ref name="斎藤"/>

Although it is difficult to accept at face value the *Shaki*’s claim that the basin was still a great lake in the Wadō era, archaeological evidence shows long habitation: the Enokida site in Chizuka, Kōfu City, is a settlement site from the {{ill|Yayoi period|Q207858|qid=Q207858}} through the {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}; the surrounding area contains the Chizuka–Yamamiya kofun group; the late-6th-century {{ill|Kamunazuka Kofun|Q11398722|qid=Q11398722}} exists nearby; and the mid-6th-century {{ill|Manjumori Kofun|Q22120416|qid=Q22120416}} is located in Yumura, Kōfu City. Thus, the area is thought to have been developed since the Yayoi and Kofun periods.<ref>*Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten 19: Yamanashi Prefecture* (Kadokawa Shoten, 1984).</ref> {{ill|Jōmon pottery|Q4390366|qid=Q4390366}} has also been excavated near the shrine, suggesting ancient ritual activity, and some associate the standing stone of just over 1 {{ill|Metre|Q11573|qid=Q11573}} behind the main hall with the shrine’s founding.<ref name="斎藤"/>

The earliest firm documentary reference to the shrine is a copy of a joint-signed certificate by the {{ill|Four Magistrates of Tokugawa|Q11490263|qid=Q11490263}} dated {{ill|Keichō|Q1328185|qid=Q1328185}} 8 ({{ill|1603|Q6735|qid=Q6735}}), granting 5 koku and 7 to of black-seal shrine land in Nishi-Aonuma Village. The *Kokushi* records the shrine land as 5 koku and 2 shō, and this holding was maintained throughout the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}}.

With the formation of the Kōfu castle town centered on {{ill|Maizuru Castle Park|Q969909|qid=Q969909}} in the Edo period, areas including parts of present-day Takara 1–2 chōme and Marunouchi 2–3 chōme, southwest of the castle, became outer samurai districts known as “Anagiri,” named after the shrine. The {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kami-Iida Daikansho}} magistrate’s office compound was also located there, and the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kōfu Josui}} waterworks drawn from the Aikawa River ran through the area. A castle gate in Hyakuseki-chō was called “Anagiri Gate” after the shrine, and the shrine enjoyed the reverence of the warrior class, including the {{ill|Kōfu Kinban|Q11577779|qid=Q11577779}}.

When hereditary succession of the {{ill|Gūji|Q11453500|qid=Q11453500}} was abolished by the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Meiji government}} the following year, the post became vacant at times, during which ancient records were lost.<ref>*History of Yamanashi Prefecture: Cultural Properties Volume*.</ref>

=== Festivals and rites ===
The annual festival is held on {{ill|April 19|Q2523|qid=Q2523}}. According to the *Kokushi*, in the early modern period the Masaki family, with residences in Shin-Aonuma Village<ref>A village separated from Nishi-Aonuma Village, corresponding to present-day Takara 1-chōme and Marunouchi 2-chōme.</ref>, held the hereditary position of {{ill|Kannushi (disambiguation)|Q15888735|qid=Q15888735}}.

=== Shrine buildings ===
=== Main hall ===
The date of construction of the main hall is unknown, but stylistically it is thought to be a reconstruction from the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Momoyama period}}.<ref>Unless otherwise noted, this section is based on *History of Yamanashi Prefecture: Cultural Properties Volume*.</ref>

It is a relatively small {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|Q210684|qid=Q210684}} one-bay shrine. A raised veranda with balustrades runs along three sides of the front and sides; *wakishōji* are set behind the core, and a pair of wooden *karado* doors is fitted at the center of the front. The bracket complexes are projecting sets of linked triple blocks with true bracket arms, with protruding *kobushibana* supporting richly colored eave purlins; the *kibana* on the head tie beams show elements of the {{ill|Zenshūyō|Q3575224|qid=Q3575224}}. The {{ill|cypress bark roof|Q90373477|qid=Q90373477}} has straight eave members at the front, showing curvature only at the eave tips, differing from medieval shrine styles that curve the entire eave.

The {{ill|kōhai|Q11415970|qid=Q11415970}} (worship porch) uses vividly colored triple-block brackets; the {{ill|kōryō|Q124421222|qid=Q124421222}} connecting the porch columns is simple in form but boldly lacquered in red and black, conveying a sense of dignity.

The porch columns are not connected to the core columns by rainbow beams, instead featuring only carved {{ill|tabasami|Q124660898|qid=Q124660898}}. From the {{ill|Munafuda|Q8008834|qid=Q8008834}}, repairs and reroofing are known to have been carried out in {{ill|Jōkyō|Q1146221|qid=Q1146221}} 4 ({{ill|1687|Q7668|qid=Q7668}}) and {{ill|Meiwa|Q1146161|qid=Q1146161}} 2 ({{ill|1765|Q7665|qid=Q7665}}). Despite its small scale, the hall retains Momoyama-period decorative characteristics in its details, particularly in the {{ill|kaerumata|Q123117911|qid=Q123117911}} and other relief carvings, which show early forms of the detailed ornamentation that developed from the Momoyama period onward. The shape of the *kibana* on the rainbow beam connecting the porch columns resembles those of shrine buildings constructed by the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Takeda clan}} in the late {{ill|Muromachi period|Q334845|qid=Q334845}}, drawing attention as an example sharing common architectural traits.

In {{ill|Shōwa era|Q327567|qid=Q327567}} 10 ({{ill|1935|Q18658|qid=Q18658}}), it was designated a National Treasure (former classification) under the {{ill|National Treasures Preservation Law|Q11420716|qid=Q11420716}}; with the enforcement of the {{ill|Cultural Properties Protection Law|Q1188502|qid=Q1188502}} on August 29, 1950, it became an {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Q1188622|qid=Q1188622}}. Three attached ridge tags (two from Jōkyō 4 and one from Meiwa 2) were additionally designated in 1962.

=== Other buildings ===
The worship hall is a reinforced-concrete {{ill|Kirizuma-style|Q13308575|qid=Q13308575}} structure with copper-sheet roofing, entered from the gable side. The former worship hall, built in {{ill|Shōtoku (era)|Q1193848|qid=Q1193848}} 5 ({{ill|1715|Q6884|qid=Q6884}}), was donated to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Fujitake Shrine}} in Nirasaki City.<ref>*Yamanashi Prefecture Shrine Gazetteer* (Yamanashi Prefecture Shinto Youth Association, 1985).</ref>
[[File:Anagiri Shrine Gate.JPG|thumb|200px|Zuijin Gate]]
The Zuijin Gate is a two-story {{ill|Rōmon|Q97378762|qid=Q97378762}} with {{ill|East Asian hip-and-gable roof|Q855025|qid=Q855025}} roofing, three bays wide with a single central opening. According to its ridge tag, it was built in {{ill|Kansei|Q1195131|qid=Q1195131}} 6 ({{ill|1794|Q7811|qid=Q7811}}) by the master carpenter Takeshita Genzō of {{ill|Shimoyama carpenters|Q11360815|qid=Q11360815}}.

The carvings were executed by {{ill|Tatekawa Kashiōrō|Q65277448|qid=Q65277448}} (Tomimune), the first master of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tatekawa school}}. Featuring excellent carvings of plants and animals such as {{ill|Order of Saint Louis|Q247777|qid=Q247777}}, young leaves, {{ill|Lion|Q140|qid=Q140}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=elephants}}, the gate particularly displays the school’s characteristics in the *shakujō*-carving beneath the rainbow beams and the “shells on waves” motif beneath the upper-story purlins. Both architecture and sculpture are outstanding, and as a valuable example of late-Edo-period gate architecture, it was designated a Kōfu City cultural property in {{ill|Heisei era|Q234510|qid=Q234510}} 13 ({{ill|2001|Q1988|qid=Q1988}}).<ref>Kōfu City Board of Education, “Anagiri Ōjinja Zuijin Gate” (on-site explanatory sign, February 2003).</ref>

The {{ill|Karahafu|Q977293|qid=Q977293}}-roofed kagura hall is thought to have been built slightly earlier than the Zuijin Gate, though the projecting wings of the roof appear to be later additions. The form of these projections has been noted as similar to the kagura hall of {{ill|Suwa-taisha|Q218813|qid=Q218813}} (Lower Shrine, Akimiya), an Important Cultural Property, which was raised in {{ill|Tenpō|de|Tempō|eo|Tenpo-epoko|fa|تنپو|fr|Ère Tenpō|ja|天保|ko|덴포|pl|Tenpō|pt|Tenpō|ru|Тэмпо|simple|Tenpō|sr|Тенпо|sv|Tenpō|tr|Tenpō|zh|天保 (日本)|qid=Q1369045}} 6 ({{ill|1835|Q7597|qid=Q7597}}).

=== Auxiliary shrines ===
In addition to Shinmei Shrine, Shiogama Shrine, and Dōso Shrine, there are several small shrines, including stone shrines dedicated to Inari Daimyōjin.
